metadata.quote: -- We’re human beings with the blood of a million savage years on our hands, but we can stop it! We can admit that we’re killers, but we’re not going to kill today. That’s all it takes...knowing that we’re not going to kill today. (from  Star Trek  Episode 23,  A Taste of Armageddon ) -- I hope I never recover from this. A Grim 'Huge Extinction Event' Happened 30 Million Years Ago, And We Only Just Noticed[1]
sections.title: Mass Extinction 30 Million Years Ago

sections.text: All right, Cara, tell us about this mass extinction 30 million years ago.
Yeah, so there are some headlines going around based on an article that was recently published in Communications Biology.
The article is called Widespread Loss of Mammalian Lineage and Dietary Diversity in the Early Oligocene of Afro-Arabia.
That describes what the article is about.
The headlines, not so much.

You might see some that say, a grim, huge extinction event happened 30 million years ago and we just only noticed, or the press release out of Duke, the climate-driven mass extinction no one had seen.
Well, we were pretty aware of this mass extinction.
The difference here is that we know that it also happened in an area where we didn't think it happened.
That's going to be the crux of this argument.
The extinction event, which is well established, is the Eocene-Oligocene extinction event.
It happened at the end of the Eocene, about 33.9 million years ago, into the beginning of the Oligocene.
And we saw a large-scale extinction of both flora and fauna.
It is somewhat small compared to the other mass extinctions that we have looked at.
Historically, we thought that most of the affected organisms were marine or aquatic.
We also saw that there was a lot of turnover in Europe and in Asia.
Notably, one of the things that went extinct during this, or one of the entire, I don't even know, is it an order?
It might even be larger than an order, that went extinct during this event are the ancient cetaceans, also known as the Archaeoceti.
And it's a group that really spawned, I guess you could say, evolutionarily, both the toothed whales and the baleen whales.
But this group itself went extinct during, of course, the toothed whales and baleen whales went on, but that group itself went extinct during this event.
So I don't know, a little trivia for your pocket.
There's a lot of question about exactly what was going on at this boundary.
We know it was a major climatic change based on, you know, looking at glacial evidence, ice core evidence, sea level evidence, you know, a lot of isotopes from the seafloor.
It doesn't seem like there was any one clear, you know, there wasn't one volcanic event or even potentially one asteroid.
It could have been several large meteorite impacts.
It could have been multiple volcanic events.
Also we saw a decrease in carbon dioxide, a change in oxygen isotopes, and a big change in the Antarctic ice sheets.
But I think most of us are pretty aware now, even if we don't study this stuff, because it is very complicated, that climate change is complex.
And a lot of things happen when, you know, some things happen.
Are these like runaway effects?
That's not really the takeaway from this study.
The takeaway from this study has to do with specifically, as was mentioned in the title, the African and Arabian continent.
So this was a time, I think, right prior to the Arabian Peninsula breaking off.
And historically, researchers thought that these areas of the globe were sort of like left alone during this Eocene-Oligocene transition.
So like I mentioned, we saw massive change, and we've known for quite some time that there was massive change in Europe and Asia.
We also saw massive change in like Antarctica, in different glacial movements.
But Africa and Arabia was largely thought to be sort of untouched.

What ended up happening here is that researchers from across the globe, in combination with Duke, they looked at a large trove of fossils, mostly from the sort of Egypt area, over a long period of collection, like decades and decades and decades of collection.
And they specifically focused on a few groups. They focused on, oh gosh, this is going to be fun. It's pronunciation time. You guys ready?
Yes.

Anomalurid and Hystricognath rodents. They focused on Carnivorous hyenodonts. So these would be extinct predatory mammals with hyena-like teeth. The Anomalodurae were these rodents that are also known as scaly-tailed squirrels. And then also I mentioned, and this one is probably narcissistically the most interesting to many of us, the Anthropoid and Stepserine primates. So these are the primate ancestors of apes and monkeys. So ultimately our ancestors. And they looked at these different groups and what they found, based on a lot of very complicated phylogenetic research, and specifically focusing on dentition, so looking at the topographic changes in teeth, they found that there was a massive bottleneck that occurred in this region of the planet. That the diversity that existed prior to the end of the Eocene and entering into the Oligocene all but disappeared. And especially with regards to the primates, only one tooth type seems to have remained. And that tooth type eventually led to all of us. And the really interesting takeaway that a lot of the researchers say is like, we may not have survived this.
We may not be here if this extinction event had wiped out our primate ancestors.
But ultimately, even though it dropped the diversity down to almost nil, some organisms survived.
Those organisms had a very particular type of tooth that ultimately led to a new diversity, right?
Because we see this happen a lot with evolutionary genetics, that there's all this diversity, there's an extinction event or a pinch point, a massive bottleneck.
The diversity goes down to almost nothing.
And then with time, we re-diversify.

And ultimately, all of the diversity that we see on the planet today with regards to monkeys and apes does seem to have come down to this one pinch point based on this one very specific type of tooth, which is pretty freaking interesting, if you ask me.
And Cara, they made the point that the tooth anatomy is a good marker for diversity, because it also reflects the diversity of what you're eating.
Yeah.
So if there's only one thing out there to eat in the ecosystem, then everyone's going to have the same tooth anatomy.
And if there's a lot of different things to eat, then that's where you get a lot of diversity in the tooth anatomy.
Yeah, and that reflects your niche.
Or for people who want to write in and complain about our pronunciation, the niche.
But yeah, it's true.
It's so much more than just anatomy.
It is ecology.
Your teeth reflect your ecology, which is a really interesting concept.
And I think what really struck me as I was looking at this article, the actual source article is how complicated the scientific endeavor of understanding evolution over large timescales really is.
Because it comes down to genetic analysis.
It comes down to geographic analysis.
It comes down to morphology.
It comes down to ecology.
All of these different factors have to be modeled together.
Well, it's not just that, Cara.
It's not just the complexity of the details that we're looking at.
It's also the fact of the patchiness of the fossil record.
We're getting glimpses in different locations and time periods represented by specific fossil beds that we find.
And so it's really challenging to do statistical analysis.
It's not like we have a continuous fossil record of like most African species over this period of time.
How could we not notice that they mostly went away?
Because we're just trying to statistically pull this out of the data from these just patchy little moments, glimpses, flashbulbs in this long, long history.
And you're right.
They're patchy both kind of horizontally in time and vertically in time.

So at any given moment, or let's say over the length of a lot of time, we are only seeing maybe something happening this many million years and then a few hundred thousand after and then maybe 10,000 after and then another 2 million after.
But then also if you're looking horizontally across time, at any given time, there are countless species that we never will know about because they never left a trace.
And that's something that's almost difficult for us to wrap our heads around.
We have this sort of paleontological idea that we sort of know about everything that ever existed because we've got evidence from it.
But there are literal whole species that never fossilized.
And one last thing before we go on.
Whales are in the order Arteodactyla.
They're in the infraorder Cetacea.
And the Archaeoceti is a parvorder, which is one notch below infraorder.
Yeah, it's an order, then infraorder, then parvorder.
And that's when you get down to the Archaeoceti.
Wow, I didn't even...
Gosh, I didn't even know that they were subdivided that deeply.
When you think about it, they came up with class, order, and gene and species.
Yeah, that's an old distinction.
It's a finite number of taxonomical levels.
But what if you need many more levels?

They had to keep inventing these different levels to put, to slice in their superorder and infraorder and parvorder to just to fit, you have to create enough levels to accommodate whatever is the reality out there.

So now certain materials can remove all of those degrees, like all of those angles, except for one for the electric field oscillation.

sections.title: Plant Molecular Farming

sections.text: All right, Jay, we're going to learn a new term here.
What is plant molecular farming?
As the global population of our planet grows, some say way too fast, our needs for food increases with it, right along with it, right?
So humanity has and still is always trying to make food production more efficient and sustainable.
So today we also want it to be environmentally friendly.
So when it comes to the future of food production, humanity is going to have to use biotechnology to help us reach our food needs.

So if you're at one end of an evolutionary branch and all of your closely related relatives died off, then it may seem like, oh, you're your own thing out there on your own.
But in order to get there, you have to leave a trail of ancestors that are a spectrum.
Species are a spectrum.
There's no sharp demarcation line.
And you can say, well, what about breeding when you don't crossbreed?
Well, but what if we occasionally crossbreed?
What if we exchange genes through an intermediary?
No matter what type of definition you come up with, you could break it.
And nature does break it.
Yeah, wolves and dogs can have viable offspring.
Yeah.
They're considered different species.
Well, they're actually not, but it's arbitrary.
Is a chihuahua and a wolf the same species?
Why would you consider them the same species?
They look so different.
Well, because, you know, they're genetically very similar.
Or anything we try to categorize, the categories break down because nature is messy and it tends to be more of a spectrum.
That's why, like, if you try to categorize everybody in the solar system as either a moon, a planet, or an asteroid, that works if you have a few...
What about X?
That breaks down.
Dwarf planets.
Is Charon, is Pluto's largest...
Planetesimals.
Yep.
That's why I love my Archaeopteryx statue that I have on my forearm.
People often ask me, why did you pick that out of all the different fossils?
And I'm like, because it's weird.
It doesn't...
It's like, it's sort of a bird dinosaur bird.
It's awesome.
I know.
Like, Dwayne Gish tried to say, either it's a dinosaur or it's a bird.
No, Mr. Gish.
It's so wrong.
It's literally not either of those.
It's in the middle.
You know nothing.
It's a bird dinosaur because it's, you know, it's like right in the middle of this transition from one to the other.
It's neither and both.
It's half of one and half of the other.
Yeah.
It breaks the category.
Literally.
I love it.
Yeah.
But the human brain likes to think in terms of discrete categories.
And we like to pretend that our categorization system, these boxes that we invent in order to help us understand and wrap our head around the universe, that they reflect reality when they don't.
Because reality is continuous and sloppy and messy and fuzzy at the edges.
Relax and Enjoy Your Food: Save your money, your health, and your sanity by separating fact from flapdoodle.

We have an excellent interview with Craig Good about his book on food.
Let's go to that interview now.
We are joined now by Craig Good.
Craig, welcome back to the Skeptics Guide.
It's great to be back and I love what you've done with this.
Thank you.
Did Bob pick the curtains?
A quick back story.
Our virtual presence.
Because we know Craig.
We have a history friendship with Craig.
So I think, Craig, you first contacted us, I mean, God, it was probably like, what, 12 years ago at this point?
Sure, something like that.
And Craig, you used to work at Pixar.
That's correct.
And Craig said something like, hey, if you guys get out here, and we were like, okay, we'll be there next week.
And we were like, immediately wanting to go and we got to see like a backstage tour of Pixar and it was one of the coolest things.
Yeah, it was incredible.
We will always remember you for that.
Thank you so much.
It was my pleasure.
That and then the free lesson you gave us on like the basics of camera, of camera, camera work, which we totally needed because we, you know, we're amateurs.
If you don't know, how are you going to learn?

Craig.
Craig.
Really?
Well, my old Craig, my Mexican family could never pronounce it at all.
So yeah, Craig.
It would come out Grek.
Grek.
Oh, cute.
I love it.
So we're having you on the show this week to talk about a new book that you just published, which you kindly sent us copies of Relax and Enjoy Your Food.
All about just some really basic science-based nuts and bolts about nutrition, food, dieting, etc.
Yeah.
So give us a quick overview.
What's the book about?
Why'd you write it?

So the book is really about having a healthy relationship with food. And I wrote it because I figured somebody had to. Nobody else was. I used to spend a lot of time on Quora, which is this question and answer site because of my interest in food and the experience I had with my daughter helping them recover from anorexia. I had a lot of interest in food and I was answering some food questions and I started noticing that 98% of the questions were the same four or five questions over and over again. So that, well, that's kind of telling me that there's a screaming need out there to just, you know, clear away the crap and figure out what's basic, you know, and that it's, you know, science is complicated, but knowing how to eat really doesn't have to be. The consensus has been pretty solid on that for a long time.
Yeah.
I mean, I agree.
And we've said that a lot on the show.
It's actually quite simple.

For most people, you don't need to have a ton of information to be like 98% of the way there in terms of having a healthful diet. It's just, there's just not a lot of money to be made on telling people the same one paragraph of information over and over again. And so the self-help industry creates a lot of food, dieting advice just as a product, even though it's not based on science.
That's what I refer to in the book as fear-based marketing. I was going to say, it preys on people's anxieties. Yeah.
It really does.
Yeah.
Make people afraid of something and then say, and here's the solution.
Craig, did you find anything during your research that surprised you that you didn't know going into it?
That's a really funny question because yes, when I was writing the book, it surprised me and today if I found it, it wouldn't surprise me at all.
And that is that it wasn't surprising that most of the anti-GMO propaganda you hear is funded by Big Organic, but most of the rest of it is funded by Russia.
What?
Yeah.
That really surprised me.
It doesn't surprise me now because it's all of a piece with anti-vax and all the other just pot stirring that they've been doing.
But that surprised me when I ran across it.
To what end?
I'll tell you because I've been encountering this for years.
I too had my awakening when I realized that this was happening, that this was a thing.
So there is a Russian propaganda outlets.
RT?
Oh, RT is the main TV show.
I don't know about the news.
No, the RT.
Yeah, RT is like the one.
So I kept getting sent these articles by RT by people that I know, Americans, people that I know in America who are at the liberal end of the political spectrum that essentially were anti-corporate.
And I'm like, so I always check sources.
And so I checked the source like, this is a Russian propaganda outlet.
Why are my liberal friends sending me Russian propaganda?
And then I did some more digging and then I learned that, oh, this is how they stir the pot.
They are stirring anti-corporate sentiment in the United States as just part of their mischief making.
So it makes absolutely perfect sense.
Yeah.
Well, that really makes me angry, to be honest with you.
But it's a part of our daily life.
The worst thing is, the worst thing is I pointed out to somebody, that link you sent me was to a Russian propaganda outlet.
And they said, well, I still agree with it.
It's like, okay.
Good for you.
Good for you.
All right.

So what are some of the, give us a couple of the biggest myths that you would like, you wish, if you could wave your magic wand and make people understand this, what are the biggest things that people need to walk away from your book with?
One way I put it is that what you eat today doesn't matter, but what you eat this month matters a lot.
Right?
I really encourage people to take the big view and not sweat the details over specific foods or ingredients or things.
So, you know, anytime someone's trying to frighten you away from a food or an ingredient, you can just ignore them.
They're almost always selling something.
Yeah, I agree.
That's one of mine as well, is that there's no good or bad food.
Right.
It's not like you can't just demonize certain foods and put a health halo around other super foods.
It's about the aggregate of your diet over time.
Exactly.
Yeah.
As long as it's balanced, you're good.
Yeah.
What I stress is variety.
For people who want to gamify it, I say, see how many different species you can eat.
SPEAKER_05 Right.
SPEAKER_05 Right.
Because if you do that, if you maximize the number of species, you're going to get a lot of fruits and veggies.
Then you get into a whole debate about what's the difference between a cultivar and a species.
Sure.
But you hear something similar when people say try to have as much color on your plate as possible.
Like, that's another approach.
Like try and avoid this sort of like beige colon cancer diet.
That helps you get variety.
That'll work.
Although it turns out to be a myth that you can tell how, quote unquote, nutritious a food is by how colorful it is.
Sure.
I don't know if that's a correlation.
But yeah, if you're getting lots of colors, you're probably getting lots of different plants.
So great.
Variety.
Greg, what about animal fat?
What are some of the fats that we should actually avoid?
You probably want to avoid trans fats and you want to kind of minimize those saturated fats.
You've talked about that on the show.
Right.
Mm-hmm.
And the best advice I think anybody can give you is to enjoy a variety of foods, mostly fruits, including plenty of fruits and veggies, not too much or too little.
And pretty much any advice more specific than that is someone selling something.
Right.
Yeah.
Although I usually add the caveat for most healthy people, right?
If you have a specific, like if you have diabetes, you need more detail than that.
Sure.
Or if you're on a cardiac diet.
So just to make, yeah.
We're not giving out medical advice.
If you're a generally healthy person, you don't need a medically specific diet and you're just interested in a general healthful diet, that's perfect advice.
Exactly.
And that's who the book is written for.
Yeah.
You don't need more detail on that.
Everything beyond that is diminishing returns.
Like not only massively diminishing returns, but in my experience, you're far more likely to degrade your diet.
You're far more likely to have a worse diet if you try to get more specific.
The biggest reason is that people start to eliminate things from their diet.
Well, and that leads also to worse mental health.

Because one of the things that I see quite often is that when people become, you know, they might become dialed into their health in a really balanced way and they feel good, but they go beyond a certain threshold of sort of obsessing over, you know, sweating over the small stuff.

Like whether it's calorie counting, which can be very healthy to a point, or whether it's, you know, like you mentioned, sort of restricting certain foods at a certain point, it becomes an issue of control.
And the more that it becomes dominating in somebody's life, the more crushing it can be for their mental health.
And we have, of course, textbook examples, DSM examples of things like anorexia and other eating disorders.
But there are a lot of shades of gray of these things and we see it all the time.
Well, that gets right to the attitude.
I don't call it a diagnosis, but an attitude in the book of orthorexia, where you confuse food with right and wrong or good and evil.
And yeah, that takes you right down that road.
It's a hard path too, once you're in that road to really learn how to let go and sort of, as I always like to say, just hold things lightly.
One part of the book that I really, really appreciated, and it's one of my favorite things to read, is...
It's where I plugged your book.
Yes.
No, it's really about the myths.
It's about the bad information that we have in our heads that we don't even really know where it came from or how it got there.
And that section was pretty meaty.
I dug it.
I read it a few times just because I wanted to try to retain as much as I could.
How hard was it to research that?
Where did that information come from?
Oh, the Mytholany chapter?
Yes, I thought it was awesome.
That I actually adapted from a Skeptoid episode I did a few years ago.
So I did the research back then.

I've long been a subscriber to Cook's Illustrated, now better known as America's Test Kitchen, which are, yeah, they're really awesome and probably the most science-based approach to cooking you're going to find out there.
And so I picked up a lot of the myths there.
And then just here and there.
I'm an old guy, so I just pick stuff up along the way.
But I tried to...
Can you give us some examples?
Like some myths that sort of most people think are true that turns out aren't based in evidence?
Oh, I'll start right at the big one.
That searing a steak seals in the juices.
That's like the most persistent cooking myth ever.
I still have trouble not believing it's true because it's been said so many times.
Well, because I still sear my steaks.
I'm not saying not to sear it.
The reason you're doing it is for flavor.
It's the Maillard reaction.
Oh, it's because I want that nice crust.
Exactly.
That's what it does.
So my favorite way to do a steak, since I've got sous vide equipment, and I think some of you do now too, right?
Is you sous vide it up to that perfect medium rare and then sear it to get the outside right and then chef's kiss.
So sous vide, just so you know, it's a...
You would essentially put the food in a bag and then you boil it.
It's like a warm water bath.
It never boils.
Well, it's not boiled.
The trick is it holds food at a super precise temperature and the doneness of meat is entirely a function of temperature.
Nothing else.
It's just what temperature the meat has reached.
So 132 Fahrenheit, I think, is medium rare.
And so you hold it in the water bath at exactly that temperature.
And the nice thing about it is that it won't overcook.
Restaurants do this all the time.

When you go to a restaurant and they're able to bring you a steak right away, it's because the steak has probably been cooking in the sous vide bath for hours at the right temperature and then they can just finish it to whatever doneness you want.
Boom, boom, boom.
That's smart.
And it comes out great.
So you're starting with all of them medium rare already and then you can just sear them off for what you need.
So I'm going to debunk a myth right now.
I am not a monster because I like my steaks well done.
Deal with it.
Deal with it.
I like it medium well.
I say whatever doneness you want.
As long as you understand that once it gets past medium, it's not really getting more cooked.
It's just the juices are just getting squeezed out more.
Interesting.
It's shrinking.
But however you want it is fine.
But it makes me feel good.
So Kara, so you like a less hydrated steak.
Yeah.
And I say enjoy the steak the way you want to enjoy your steak.
Thank you.
I appreciate that.
All right.
Let me push back on that a little bit only because what you said is correct if you're using that method.
But if you're grilling your steak, it refers to the temperature you get down to in the middle.
In the middle, yeah.
Yeah.
So if you don't like that pink center, then you have to get it at least medium well to get rid of the... to get the center cooked.
So it's just a different...
It depends on how you're cooking the steak.
Right.
Yeah.
The doneness in that case varies.
The big thing with sous vide is that you get a very consistent doneness whichever one you want.
Right.
And if you're doing chicken, I do the opposite.
I cook the outside until the outside's done.
Then I bake it to get the whole thing to the right temperature.
Well, that's how I cook steak.
Yeah.
And that steak method can work well too.
You can do it in either order you want.
Ah, interesting.
It's a combination of fast and slow.
But it's not sealing in juices.

What are some other myths more about... less about, I guess, cooking and more about like nutrition, like things that we all think we're supposed to be doing or shouldn't be doing, which are either perfectly fine or probably not that great?
Kind of depends on where you live.
A lot of the questions on Quora came from India.
And Ayurveda has some of the craziest beliefs like you can't eat bananas combined with eggs.
Well, we don't want to do that.
Well, I put bananas on my French toast all the time.
That's bananas.
Oh, you're right.
And Craig, it's funny that you say that because when I am trying to lose weight, I will have a couple of hard boiled eggs and a banana for breakfast.
So I'm like, I'm breaking the rules over here.
Yeah, it's fine.
You can eat any food in combination with any other food you like.
There's no magic to it.
One thing that helps I explain in the book is that food all, it all just really is sorted into the same seven buckets when you eat it.
You're either getting carbs, proteins, fats, or hydration, vitamins, minerals, or fiber.
And that's all food is, is something that gives you one or more of those things.
And it's all good.
It can all be part of a healthy diet.
That's that other myth that won't die is that you need eight glasses of water a day.
Oh, right.
Yeah.
That one just, I was like, please, kill it with fire.
Where did that even come from?
It came from a memo someone wrote in the 40s.
And people forget the context where he said, right after that, and most of that you get from your diet.
Right.
That's all sources of water.
Most of the water you need, you get from your food.
Like bread.
Bread has water in it, believe it or not.
Well, it's not just that.
It's just a representative.
I debunked this too in my medical myth lecture for the teaching company.
But it's like, there's no one amount for everybody in every situation.
That's what I was thinking.
Like, how could a 95 pound, 75 year old woman need the same amount as a 400 pound, 32 year
old man? Yeah.
In the summer versus the winter, exercise, no exercise, whatever.
It's how about this, just drink when you're, as long as you're not like doing extreme performance things or exercising or in the desert, just drink when you're thirsty and you'll be fine.
That's all you have to do, is drink when you're thirsty.
Understand thirst, right?
Like, because I think some people, they're thirsty and they eat.
And so that can be a difficulty.
Like you do need to drink when you're thirsty.
Yeah.
Except Scientologists, because they could detect hunger.
That's one of their superpowers.
So what about food in terms of diet and losing weight?
Right, that's where I'm at right now, Bob.
Okay.
So I've got a little chapter on that.
One thing to remember is there's no such thing as a fattening food.
And there also no such thing as a weight loss food.
It's really a matter of thermodynamics.
So if you run a consistent calorie deficit, you're going to lose weight, because it has to come from somewhere.
So it's simple, but it's not necessarily easy for everybody.
I think the key is mostly recognizing what the calorie density is of different foods you eat.
Yes.

And there's a little tweak you can give your diet that actually, credit to another book, I'm not going to blank on the name of it, but I mentioned it in my book, where all you need is to get some more veggies.
And if you just serve your veggie course first, they've shown that you will eat more veggies.
They even tested this in school cafeterias.
If they put the vegetables first in the line, kids ended up eating more vegetables.
It's just a simple little hack.
Why?
Would they serve themselves more vegetables because of that?
Yeah, because you're going by putting stuff on your plate, you know.
And I would assume too that your meal is made up of, it's a zero sum game.
You only eat however many calories in a single meal.
So if you start with all of your vegetables, you're going to get fuller faster and you're going to be less likely then to eat a larger percentage of other foods.
Yeah, you'll get just some bulking because vegetables tend to be very low calorie density.

The other thing you can do, and it turns out a friend of a friend did this and it's almost a page literally out of the book, where I showed that if you have the habit of having a lot of sweet drinks during the day, if you have a couple of fruit juices or soda pop, which nutritionally are essentially the same thing, pop and juice are just sugar water.
If you're used to that and you just cut that out, that's often enough to make the difference.
And this particular guy, he had spent years of his life like 50 pounds overweight.
And then he realized, oh, it's because to get the caffeine I wanted, I was having a couple of liters of Coke a day.
So I just start- Regular Coke, wow.
Or a liter of Coke.
He was having a bunch of Coke.
And he just stopped doing that.
And his weight dropped and he looks great.
So it can be that simple.
But what I would really warn people against are weight loss products or programs, because they're almost always a ripoff.
The wellness and diet industry, it's aimed particularly at women, but they go after everybody.
And they know that diets don't work.
And that's one of the big things to remember is diets do not work.
It's lifestyle.
Because diet is a temporary change and you're not going to get a permanent effect from a temporary change in behavior.
You go back to your, you hit your goal weight, go back to eating the way you used to, and you're back up to the weight you used to be.
And probably worse off.
Yeah.
And often worse off.
Yeah.
Right.
The yo-yoing can be much worse.
Well, one thing to remember is that being overweight isn't as dangerous as people think.
That's true too.
Being overweight will give you bad outcomes and kill you slowly.
And being severely underweight will kill you pretty quickly.
Yeah.
Do you recommend tools though?
Because I will tell you, I use tools.
I use calorie counting tools.
And they really do help me.
I use a calorie counting tool.
I use an app called Lose It.
I use an app.
I use MyFitnessTracker.
MyFitnessTracker.
Yeah.
They're pretty similar.
I got to give the caveat that Lose It sometimes promotes some really wooey stuff like DNA analysis and stuff.
That sucks.
I hate that.
But as a calorie counter, it works fine.
I recommend that if you aren't obsessive about numbers.
For some people, if you've had an eating disorder, I would not recommend counting calories.
Of course.
Yeah.
But if you're a geek like me, I like charts and graphs and tracking stuff.
So I weigh everything I eat and I'm able to keep a pretty steady thing.
And the error bars around it are huge.
I mean, the calories on the labels are legally allowed to be plus or minus 20%.
Oh my God.
What?
But I think the most useful thing about calorie counting is even if you just do it for a while, I think most people have no idea how many calories are in the thing.
Exactly.
That's what I was going to say too.
But if you're in the kitchen for a while and you realize, wow, this large french fry is 1900 calories.
This thing right here is my calories for the day.
It's just insane.
And if you don't know that, it's super easy to massively overdo.
Well, Craig, we really recommend the book.
It's a fun read.
Thank you.
Not just the part where you plug our book.
Thank you for that.
And we're happy to return the favor.
It's good.
It's a small, quick, easy read.
It's a good reference.
It's a good introduction for people who have never encountered any science-based information about nutrition or dieting.
And you're right.
Most things that most people believe about food and dieting, whatever, is wrong.
It's misinformation that was peddled by somebody to make money.
This is one of those areas of what we do as skeptics where correcting misinformation is actually useful and can be effective.
Yeah.
So good work.
Thank you.
Are you working on any new projects?
Not books like this.
I've got a crazy screenplay I'm working on, mostly as therapy.
But that's different.
But yeah, I've got a—it's available on Amazon.
You can get paperback, Kindle, or audio book read by the author.
Nice.
You can also go—if you read paper or listen to the audio book and want to get the footnotes, they're at relaxandenjoyyourfood.com.
I just put up pages of footnotes there for people who want to follow along.
Oh, cool.
Yeah, because I'm trying to encourage people to explore and read other stuff too.
Yeah, for sure.
Great.
All right.
Well, thanks for joining us, Greg.
Thank you so much.
Thanks, Greg.
